issues.legal_issue: Agrarian reform measures that reduce land ceilings and confer protected cultivation rights on tillers are constitutionally valid when they distribute agricultural resources for the common good.
material_facts: The challenged amendments reduced the agricultural land that former landlords could retain and provided for cultivation by bargadars, including protection of bargadars’ rights.
The amendments provided for surplus agricultural land to be distributed among landless tillers, while leaving owners homestead land, buildings and land within the applicable ceiling.
The petitioners argued that the amendments caused confiscatory deprivation, lacked a sufficient connection to distributive objectives, and involved no genuine distribution.
issues.conclusion: The amendments were valid. They were directed to distributing agricultural resources among tillers for the common good, and the broad conception of distribution includes the allocation of resources in this manner. The challenge based on confiscation, lack of nexus, or absence of a distribution process therefore failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of the material resources of the community to serve the common good; distribution is not confined to literal division and includes allocation and apportionment. Article 31C protects laws that give effect to Article 39(b) from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The Court applied Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India, Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Waman Rao v. Union of India, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai, and Sasanka Sekhar Maity v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law reforming agricultural land ownership or cultivation.
predicates.surplus_agricultural_land_is_allocated_t: The law reallocates surplus agricultural land to people who till the land.
predicates.reform_is_directed_to_serving_the_common: The reform is directed to distributing community resources for the benefit of the community.

issues.definition: When a challenged agrarian reform reallocates surplus agricultural land to tillers for the common good, the reform is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: A requirement that an owner-cultivator reside in the locality of the land for most of the year is not arbitrary or unduly harsh when it advances effective cultivation and the common good.
material_facts: The challenged law required the landowner or a family member to reside in the locality where the land was situated for the greater part of the year.
The law linked that requirement to cultivation of the land and to ensuring that the cultivator gave adequate attention to it.
issues.conclusion: The residence requirement was not harsh or arbitrary. It was a beneficial measure intended to ensure attention to cultivation and to promote effective use of agricultural resources.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 39(b) and Article 31C, concluding that a law advancing Article 39(b) could not be challenged under Articles 14, 19 or 31, and that requiring residence near the land supported cultivation and productive use. It applied Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India.

issues.legal_issue: An erroneous assumption that a land reform law is protected from challenge by its inclusion in a constitutional schedule does not invalidate the law if it is independently valid as a measure giving effect to distributive objectives.
material_facts: A previous decision had proceeded on the mistaken assumption that the relevant land reform laws had been included in the constitutional schedule before a specified date and were therefore immune from certain challenges.
The Court acknowledged that the laws had instead been added to the schedule later, so that assumed immunity did not apply.
The Court nevertheless found that the challenged provisions were reasonable and were directed to distributing agricultural resources for the common good.
issues.conclusion: The earlier assumption about schedule-based immunity was erroneous, but the amendments remained constitutionally valid on their own merits and the challenge failed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the schedule-based ground of immunity was unavailable on the facts, but that the provisions were independently supportable under Article 39(b) and the protection of Article 31C. It relied on Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India and the principles in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Waman Rao v. Union of India, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., and State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai.
